comments.content:
The implementation is correct and efficient: ownership of `String` is taken and moved back without cloning for the common (non-"user") case. The function appropriately handles the legacy "user" → "user_stated" normalization at the read-side, which is the right place per the comment's rationale (avoids touching on-disk data, edits will persist the normalized value).

Minor consideration (not a bug): the contract string `"user_stated"` is duplicated as a magic string in `is_protected` (line 168) and now here. Extracting a `const SOURCE_USER_STATED: &str = "user_stated"` (and possibly `SOURCE_USER_LEGACY: &str = "user"`) would centralize the contract, but this would be a refactor across the file and is out of scope for this change.

Non-deterministic fallback_color: `hash(pkey)` is salted per-process by PYTHONHASHSEED (random since Python 3.3), so the same provider_key maps to a different palette slot on every fresh install / replica / test reset. The color is only set on initial INSERT (the `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET` clause deliberately omits `fallback_color`/`fallback_char`), so the assignment is sticky after first sync — but two developers or two user machines get inconsistent colors for the same provider, breaking screenshots, docs, and any cross-instance UI comparison. Use a stable hash (e.g. `hashlib.blake2b(pkey.encode(), digest_size=4).digest()` interpreted as int, or `zlib.crc32(pkey)`) so the mapping is reproducible.

comments.content: SQLite connections are never closed. `with get_db() as conn:` only handles transaction commit/rollback — `sqlite3.Connection.__exit__` does NOT call `.close()`. Every request handler opens a fresh connection that is never explicitly closed; CPython refcounting will eventually collect it, but the underlying file descriptor and any prepared statements linger. For a local-only service this is not critical, but it is a real resource-management bug that will surface if this file is ever copy-pasted into a busier service. Wrap the connection in `contextlib.closing` (or add `conn.close()` in a `finally`).
comments.suggestion_code:
def get_db() -> sqlite3.Connection:
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    conn.close  # expose close so callers can use closing(get_db()) if they want
    return conn
comments.existing_code:
def get_db() -> sqlite3.Connection:
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return conn

comments.content: Silent embedding loss when embed::embed_text returns None: the SQL CASE `embedding = CASE WHEN content <> ?1 THEN ?6 ELSE COALESCE(?6, embedding) END` in store::update_by_id overwrites the embedding column with NULL whenever the engine fails (engine uninitialized, tokenizer error, ONNX session fail, dimension mismatch). The panel user sees `hasEmbedding: false` on success with no error code — they cannot tell whether the entry just lost semantic recall or was always embedding-less. Either fail closed at the command layer (return a typed error so the UI can toast "编辑已保存，但语义检索已失效" or refuse the save) or pre-check `embed::engine_status()` before issuing the update.

`update_core` reads the full table twice per edit: once to find `existing` (used only for `existing.source`) and once to read back the post-update row. Each `load_all` also deserializes the 512-dim `Vec<f32>` for every row in the table. With `MAX_MEM_ITEMS=500` this is acceptable; cleaner solution is a `store::find_by_id` (or `get_source`) helper plus returning the updated row from `update_by_id`.

let existing = store::load_all(conn)?
        .into_iter()
        .find(|m| m.id == id)
        .ok_or_else(|| "记忆不存在或已被删除".to_string())?;
    store::update_by_id(
        conn,
        id,
        content,
        importance,
        &existing.source,
        kind,
        embedding,
        now_ms,
    )?;
    let updated = store::load_all(conn)?
        .into_iter()
        .find(|m| m.id == id)
        .ok_or_else(|| "更新后读取失败".to_string())?;
    Ok(MemItemView::from(&updated))

comments.content: All backend errors are flattened to `String` at the `&Connection`-pure core layer, then wrapped as `CommandError::DbError(String)`. The frontend toast cannot distinguish "not found" (the `update_core` / `delete_core` "记忆不存在" path) from a real DB failure, and `mem_delete`'s `false` (id missing) and an `Err(...)` look identical after wrapping. Use typed errors: `TaskNotFound(id)` / `InvalidArgument { field, value, reason }` from `error.rs`.

`delete_core` does not check `store::is_protected` and has no audit trail. The file comment justifies this ("前端 confirm 文案负责提示影响"), but a frontend bug, a stale UI, or a replayed IPC can drop a protected `importance=5 user_stated` entry (or any `evo:` self-evolved lesson) with no log line. Either refuse + require an explicit `force` flag for protected rows, or return the `MemItemView` of the row being deleted so the command layer can log kind/source/importance before dropping it.

`list_core`'s kind filter does exact-string match without checking `EDITABLE_KINDS`, so a typo or stray whitespace (e.g., `"FACT "`) returns empty silently instead of erroring. Inconsistent with `update_core` which enforces the whitelist. Either validate the same way on read, or document that the read path is permissive.

`update_core` re-derives `existing.source` from `load_all` (which goes through `normalize_source`) and writes it back verbatim via `update_by_id` (which writes raw). So a row whose on-disk source is the legacy `'user'` value gets re-saved as `'user'` — not normalized. The panel cannot be used to migrate legacy dirty values; the read-side normalization in `store.rs` is load-bearing here. Either accept this and document it, or normalize once on the way through the panel.

comments.content: Test `legacy_user_source_normalized_and_protected` inserts via raw SQL and a hardcoded RFC3339 string (`'2026-01-01T00:00:00+00:00'`), bypassing `store::ts_to_text` / `ts_to_ms`. If the storage format ever changes (precision, timezone normalization), the test silently breaks. Use the store helpers to construct timestamps.

`mem_list`'s kind filter is matched against the magic string `"all"`, which is a UI sentinel leaking into the API contract. Consider a typed `Option<MemKind>` newtype or documenting the sentinel so future maintainers don't have to grep for the literal.

The pencil (edit) IconButton is not gated by `busy`, but the trash icon is. During an in-flight `mem_update` or `mem_delete`, the user can click edit on another row — `startEdit` overwrites the local `editContent`/`editKind`/`editImportance` state, then the in-flight save's `setEditingId(null)` fires, and the user sees the row they just clicked edit on snap back to display mode with no explanation. Add `disabled={busy}` to the edit button to mirror the delete button.

                  disabled={busy}

comments.content: `stats_core` calls `store::load_all(conn)`, which deserializes the entire table including the 512-dim `Vec<f32>` embedding for every row (500 × 512 × 4B ≈ 1MB at capacity). The function then only consumes `items.len()`, `m.kind`, `m.source`, and `m.embedding.is_some()` — none of which need the embedding bytes. The deserialization also runs inside `lock_db()` in `mem_stats` (single-writer gate), so every concurrent write is blocked for the duration of the embedding allocation/copy that the stats query never reads. Replace with SQL aggregates (e.g. `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mem_items`, `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mem_items WHERE embedding IS NOT NULL`, plus `GROUP BY kind` / `GROUP BY source` `COUNT(*)`) and skip `load_all` entirely.

Dead key / shadowed intent in fallback response: the explicit `"provider_key": None` is immediately overridden by `**provider_fallback("?")` (dict spread applies after the explicit key in Python literals), so `provider_key` in the response is always the string `"?"` rather than `None`. The other model-side fields stay `None`, which is inconsistent and likely not what was intended. Either drop the `"provider_key": None` line if `"?"` is the desired sentinel, or build the provider block without `provider_key` (e.g. `{k: v for k, v in provider_fallback("?").items() if k != "provider_key"}`) so the `None` actually takes effect.

Defensive null check: TypeScript's `tags: string[]` is a compile-time guarantee only. If the backend ever returns `tags: null` / `tags: undefined` (e.g., older row shape, partial migration), `m.tags[0]` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (0)`, taking down the whole delete-confirm flow. Use optional chaining so the `evo:` detection degrades gracefully.
comments.existing_code: const fromEvolution = (m.tags[0] ?? "").startsWith("evo:");

comments.content: `reload`'s success branch resets `loadError` but leaves `rowError` untouched. A stale row-level error from a previous failed `mem_update` / `mem_delete` will keep rendering in red after the user types into the search box or switches the kind filter, even though the latest reload succeeded. The two error states have different scopes (initial load vs. row operation) but they're presented as one stacked block — the user can't tell which is current. Either clear `rowError` here too, or scope the row error to the specific row (keyed by `editingId` / last-acted id) so the message doesn't bleed into unrelated interactions.

The in-flight token (reqIdRef) recommended by Finding 2 handles stale results, but does not cover unmount-during-fetch. If the Settings page is closed (or this panel unmounted) while a `reload` is mid-flight, the resolved `setItems` / `setStats` / `setLoadError` calls will fire on an unmounted component and trigger React's "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component" warning. Add a mounted ref alongside the reqIdRef check, or fold the unmount check into the same `if (stale) return;` guard. Same applies to `saveEdit` and `removeItem` — they don't guard against unmount either.
